title: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason On Building Legal AI In Real Time with Customers in Its New Innovation Lab
author: Greg Dickason

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source shifts attention from buyer-side market mapping and disciplined vendor selection to vendor-side customer co-development as a route to faster, workflow-led product delivery. This is compatible with tailoring tools to real legal needs, but it neither assesses the expanding market nor supports the cluster’s selection, adoption, cost or capability-scrutiny claims.
qs: Instead of developing products internally and asking customers to validate them afterwards, customers bring their pain points into the lab, engineers code against them on the spot, and prototypes that pass muster can move  into Lexus Plus with Protege in a matter of weeks.

In our conversation, recorded just ahead of the launch, Dickison explains what actually happens inside the lab, including watching a solution get revised four times in a single hour based on live customer feedback.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Dickason accepts the value of contextual, workflow-specific legal systems and materially extends the cluster by describing a concrete customer-embedded development model: customers define real workflows, engineers iterate directly with them, and a technology provider tests feasibility. The content-grounded query and drafting project illustrates this approach, though the source does not substantively address human verification or autonomous deployment.

His claims are technical and directional, however, and do not substantively address error propagation, verification costs, governance or measured reliability.

kp.k: Live customer collaboration compresses legal-AI development cycles
kp.d: Dickason describes a physical New York lab bringing law firms and legal departments together with LexisNexis engineers, AI labs and infrastructure providers. Its distinctive mechanism is live refinement rather than repeated build-and-feedback cycles lasting weeks or months. He reports observing four revisions in one hour; this is an operational anecdote, not a comparative study. He estimates product development is already five times faster than five years earlier and argues for another fivefold acceleration.
qs: For me, the biggest thing is we're collapsing the distance between the people who know what the problem is and the people who can build the solution, which is our engineers and our AR data scientists.
That cycle can take weeks, if not months.
So last week we saw that it live, I saw a solution get changed four times in one hour as a result of customer feedback.
But I think we need to go another five times faster, Bob.

kp.k: Rapid prototypes still require testing and production handoffs
kp.d: Dickason says functionality built on the existing platform can reach production in less than a month, but one customer's approval is insufficient and multiple customer iterations may be necessary. Content reformulation and model tuning can take longer. At interview time, sessions had run for about a month and a half; integrating a lab of approximately twenty people with engineering teams of approximately four thousand was part of the operating model being refined.
qs: It can be less than a month, but your assumption is a hundred percent correct.
We're not we're not expecting just because we've got one set of feedback from one customer that's gonna go live.
If it's if it's a content reformulation or a model tuning or something like that, that might take longer.
Because the lab's, you know, only you know, twenty or so people, whereas the engineering teams are four thousand or so.

kp.k: Co-development spans firm sizes and proprietary internal platforms
kp.d: Dickason says participation includes noncustomers, legal departments, large firms, small firms, solo practitioners, junior associates, partners, CIOs and a judge. Ordinary lab work enhances LexisNexis products, with participants acknowledging its ownership of resulting IP. He distinguishes separate collaborations helping larger firms build internal platforms that reflect their particular capabilities and AI strategies.
qs: So we've got people who are not even our customers.
We've got people from CIO level, you know, partner level, all the way down to junior associates at large law firms, small law, solo operators, even a judge.
So the IP is owned by us ~ and and people acknowledge it before they come into the lab.
That's where we are looking at at at potentially helping law firms build their own internal systems where we can we can plug in and help them.

kp.k: Multimodal vaults extend analysis beyond legal text
kp.d: Dickason identifies customer-content vaults and work on multimodal vaults as lab outputs. He describes querying documents, audio and video together to inform arguments and drafting, linked back to LexisNexis content. Video analysis was close to going live, not described as fully deployed. His example of identifying apparent surprise during a deposition illustrates proposed functionality rather than evidence of its accuracy.
qs: And we're looking now at multimodal vaults where we can store anything and and at and at pretty much any scale.
what I'm excited about is the ability to analyze videos, for example, that came out of the lab as an idea and we worked through and it's ~ close to going live.
tell me when the witness showed surprise and what was being talked about at that time, because that then can be potentially be something I can drill into.

kp.k: Drafting improvements target residual lawyer work, not complete replacement
kp.d: Asked why drafting remains a priority despite many competing tools, Dickason reports that customers feel outputs reach eighty or ninety percent of readiness but still require substantial work. He identifies firm style, playbooks, risk identification, consistency across successive documents, tracked changes and version history as gaps. These percentages are customer impressions reported by a vendor executive, not benchmark results. He explicitly retains lawyer review rather than promising fully autonomous finalisation.
qs: customers feel like they're getting to eighty, maybe ninety percent from regardless of vendor, but they're still having to do a fair amount of work post that to get it to that hundred percent where they're ready to send it out.
I'm not saying we'll ever get to a hundred because I think your your lawyer always wants to sit down and make absolutely sure that it's what they want, it's in their style and everything else.
It's one thing to do one document right. It's another thing to do multiple documents in order, right?
Then obviously there's things like track changes, version history.

kp.k: Drafting trust depends on checkable citations and contextual analytics
kp.d: Dickason presents readily accessible source links, citation checking and risk highlighting as ways to reduce hallucinations and accelerate human verification. He also proposes using Lex Machina and other intelligence to check contextual assertions such as expected time to trial. These are described priorities and capabilities, without measured reductions in errors or review time.
qs: How do we surface trust and make sure that they can verify very quickly within the draft that this is good law, that it is good citations and they can click through and see that on our platform.
we can run analytics from Lex Mackina and and other intelligence to say actually it might take longer or might take less.
So looking at the draft from the context of of the lawyers workflow ~ and some of the facts they may be stating and making sure that those are accurate as well.

kp.k: Model strategy prioritises grounded frontier models over wholesale replacement
kp.d: Dickason says LexisNexis has evaluated models for more than three years and already uses fine-tuned models for certain workflow components. His current position is that frontier models combined with appropriate prompting, context, knowledge graphs and retrieval generally deliver state-of-the-art results. Proprietary models remain under investigation, including for cost reasons, but he does not commit to replacing frontier models and identifies quality as the primary criterion.
qs: We've been evaluating models since you know, we did them with Amazon on bedrock over three years ago.
in some cases we do use fine tune models for certain parts of the legal workflow.
some of the reasons why you're looking at your own models can be from a cost perspective, and that does make sense that you can get the same quality.
So we gonna make sure the highest quality is for us the number one bar.

kp.k: Agentic loops support long-running, context-updating legal workflows
kp.d: Dickason argues that agentic systems represent a breakthrough for multifaceted transactions lasting potentially multiple months. A harness supplies changing context from research, the web, customer content and incoming communications; the model reasons about next steps and requests additional information. He links recent harness improvements to longer-running tasks and packaged Word, PowerPoint and Excel outputs. These are his assessments of technical potential, not reported outcome studies.
qs: They go for potentially a long time, you know, multiple months even if you're doing an MA or a complicated transaction.
the ability for that to be an agentic loop, I think is an absolute breakthrough compared to where we were a year ago or so.
It's the harness is giving the model, this is what's going on now. What should I do next?
And then finally producing great outputs, you know, Word documents, PowerPoints, ~ s Excel spreadsheets, things that the lawyer can use that are nicely all packaged up together and well formatted.

kp.k: Uneven AI understanding makes customer education a development function
kp.d: Dickason contrasts technically sophisticated customers using agentic tools with customers still treating AI as chat. He estimates sixty or seventy percent are not yet at the former stage, without specifying a sample or measurement method. He views the lab as an educational setting demonstrating training and harnesses. Ambrogi raises technologically advanced participant self-selection; Dickason agrees but says targeted drafting recruitment also brings in less technical practitioners.
qs: But I'd say probably sixty or seventy percent aren't there yet. They're still interacting as if it's a chat.
And and I do see the lab as a great place for from that perspective, from an education perspective.

some of our recruitment though has gone and found people who are we want to talk about drafting. Can you come in and talk to us about drafting? And then you get people who are not as technical and you get a a different different insight then.

kp.k: Personal agents may disintermediate legal-software interfaces
kp.d: Dickason predicts increasing use of personal agents acting on users' behalf. He favours MCP or agent-to-agent connections to LexisNexis's own agents rather than external agents browsing raw platform content, arguing that the latter loses grounding and tuning. He describes this interoperability as future work, not an already completed arrangement. Separately, he says the product already surfaces in Microsoft Copilot and Teams, reflecting a strategy of meeting lawyers within existing workflows.
qs: I I do think increasingly we're gonna see agents sort of disintermediating the user and agents acting on behalf of the user and we're working on how that works in our system.
And if Claude is just getting raw content and trying to pull that together That generally doesn't work. It's not well grounded.
So what we were looking at more is the MCP or agent to agent interface. So that that will work eventually.
our products can come to you in different forms.

kp.k: Workflow redesign requires simpler interfaces despite accelerating innovation
kp.d: Dickason says firms are reconsidering who performs work, when it happens and whether it occurs at intake. He argues that vendors must understand practitioners' days, practice areas and seniority rather than merely add features. His proposed balance is continuing rapid underlying innovation while agents expose relevant functionality through simpler interfaces, avoiding an accumulation of buttons and repeated user-facing disruption.
qs: a lot of law firms are reinventing how they see work happening.
who does the work, when is the work done, does it happen on intake?
I think the interface has got to get simpler.
we can't have a hundred buttons because we've had a hundred great customer sessions and each one's given us a new insight because obviously that just overwhelms you.

kp.k: Delegated work remains tied to human-checkable legal grounding
kp.d: In response to Ambrogi's suggestion that LexisNexis could become a platform lawyers assign work to rather than search, Dickason says this is potentially the direction of travel. He conditions that vision on traceable trust signals enabling users to check the result. He identifies linked content, editorial work, a point-of-law graph and robust search as the company's differentiating foundation whether a human or an agent requests an answer or draft.
qs: I think potentially we are. There's always going to be that trust layer.
So yes, you can assign work to it, it does the work, but it also gives you back the trust signals.

Because it's not just the content, it's all the work we've done in linking that, all the editorial work we've done in pulling that together, creating a knowledge graph, you know, what we call a point of law graph, having a really good, robust search system.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Greg Dickason claims that live collaboration between legal customers, engineers and AI technology providers accelerates legal-AI development and makes solutions more responsive to actual workflows.
pts.d: Dickason describes the innovation lab as shortening iterative refinement from weeks or months to repeated changes within a session. He estimates that LexisNexis already produces products roughly five times faster than five years earlier, partly through internal use of agents, and says it needs another fivefold acceleration. The further acceleration is an ambition, rather than a reported result. Some functionality developed in the lab can reach production within a month.

pts.k: Dickason says multimodal AI can interrogate firms' documents, audio and video together to identify material relevant to legal arguments and drafting.
pts.d: He identifies multimodal vaults as a lab development close to launch. His illustrative use case is querying a two-hour deposition for moments when a witness appeared surprised and identifying the associated discussion, so that a lawyer can investigate further. This is presented as a proposed investigative capability, not a demonstrated measure of emotion-detection accuracy.

pts.k: Dickason claims that existing AI drafting tools get lawyers much of the way to a usable draft, but substantial finishing and verification work remains.
pts.d: He characterizes customers as reaching roughly 80–90% completion with tools across vendors, while still spending hours on revision. These percentages describe perceived draft readiness, not measured accuracy. He identifies unmet needs in firm style and playbooks, risk highlighting, citation verification, consistency across documents, tracked changes, version history and analytics-supported factual checks. He does not promise fully autonomous final drafting: lawyers still need to check that the result meets their requirements.

pts.k: Dickason argues that frontier models combined with legal context, retrieval and knowledge graphs currently deliver leading performance; specialized models may offer cost advantages for particular tasks.
pts.d: He says LexisNexis already uses fine-tuned models for some workflow components and continually investigates its own models. He does not announce a general replacement of frontier models. His stated priority is the highest quality, with cost savings from proprietary models attractive only if equivalent quality can be maintained. He attributes the platform's grounding and trust proposition to legal content, editorial linking, search and its point-of-law graph.

pts.k: Dickason predicts that agentic loops will enable longer-running legal workflows and increasingly packaged work products, rather than just individual chat responses.
pts.d: He describes agents repeatedly incorporating research, customer content, web material and new emails, reasoning about the next action and seeking additional information. He calls this a breakthrough for multifaceted matters, including transactions lasting months. Outputs can include Word documents, presentations and spreadsheets. He sees a potential shift from searching a platform to assigning it work, but retains a lawyer-facing verification layer rather than advocating unchecked reliance.

pts.k: Dickason predicts that personal agents and embedded integrations will increasingly mediate lawyers' access to legal platforms.
pts.d: He anticipates agent-to-agent or MCP interfaces, with personal agents acting for users. He distinguishes this from letting an external agent browse raw platform content, which he says loses the grounding and tuning supplied by the platform's own agents. He also foresees simpler user interfaces that infer needs while capabilities continue to expand underneath, and tools appearing within lawyers' existing workflows rather than requiring visits to a separate product.

pts.k: Dickason describes uneven AI maturity among legal users and firm-specific efforts to redesign how work is performed.
pts.d: He estimates that 60–70% of the customers under discussion still interact with AI as chat rather than understanding agentic workflows. More technically sophisticated users are already asking more demanding questions. He says some large firms are building their own AI platforms to express distinctive capabilities, while firms are reconsidering who does work and when it happens, including at intake. He makes no quantified prediction about lawyer displacement, staffing reductions or billing-model change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims principally rest on Dickason's executive experience, customer feedback, observed lab sessions and descriptions of internal development and model evaluation.
pts.d: Concrete examples include witnessing four revisions in one hour, developing multimodal vault functionality with customers and a technology provider, and using an engineer to prototype during customer discussions. Draft-readiness and adoption percentages are informal estimates without a stated sample or methodology. Model-quality claims reference ongoing evaluation and existing fine-tuning, but no named benchmark, scores or comparative study is supplied. Claims about future agent-mediated work are projections from current capabilities, not reported longitudinal outcomes. Sponsor advertising and statements introduced only by the host are not treated as Dickason's evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Near-term development claims are tied to an early-stage lab and conditional release timelines; wider agentic transformation has no fixed deadline.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026 source, Dickason says lab sessions began about a month and a half before the interview. Functional prototypes may ship in less than a month, but require testing with multiple customers; content reformulation and model tuning may take longer, and not every prototype becomes a product. Video analysis is described as close to launch. Agentic advances are situated relative to the preceding year and especially six months. Personal-agent integration is described as eventual. Continued human checking, legal grounding, quality preservation and simple interfaces qualify the broader automation vision.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are lawyers and legal departments using AI, large firms developing proprietary workflows, and the legal-technology teams building and integrating those tools.
pts.d: Dickason describes participation across large and small firms, solo practitioners, corporate legal departments, senior leadership, junior associates and a judge, including noncustomers. Lawyers may gain faster drafting, richer analysis and delegated workflow execution while retaining verification duties. Large firms can collaborate on their own platforms, distinct from enhancements to LexisNexis products. Less technically experienced users need education about agents. Engineers gain direct exposure to legal problems, and LexisNexis must adapt to a market where access may occur through third-party agents. The interview does not develop an access-to-justice claim or quantify effects on clients' fees or legal employment.
